prompt: Each card describes how a jurisdiction governs AI. Sort each card by the regulatory model it follows.

cards.text: A country passes one AI statute that sorts every AI system, in any industry, into risk classes with matching duties.
cards.explanation: A single cross-cutting framework governs all industries by risk level.

cards.text: A country has no AI statute. Its banking regulator applies existing lending law to credit models, and its labour regulator applies employment law to hiring tools.
cards.explanation: Existing domain-specific statutes and regulators govern algorithms industry by industry.

cards.text: A country relies on a general privacy law with automated-decision rights, plus separate AI guidance issued by its health and finance ministries.
cards.explanation: Horizontal data protection and automated decision-making law combined with sectoral guidelines.

cards.text: A tenant-screening algorithm is policed by the housing agency under fair-housing law, and a medical triage tool by the health regulator under medical device rules.
cards.explanation: Each domain's own regulator applies its own statute.

cards.text: A country's privacy statute covers automated decisions for all firms, while industry bodies adopt a technical AI management standard for their members.
cards.explanation: A horizontal privacy law paired with technical management standards is the hybrid model.

cards.text: One national AI office supervises chatbots, credit scoring and factory robots under the same risk-based law.
cards.explanation: One statute and one supervisory structure span every sector.

prompt: Each case describes an AI system offered in the European Union. Identify its risk tier under the EU AI Act.

cases.text: A city scores residents on their everyday behaviour and uses the score to rank access to public services.
cases.explanation: Social scoring is a prohibited practice.

cases.text: A staffing firm uses a model to rank job applicants' résumés before any recruiter reads them.
cases.explanation: Recruitment systems are high risk and need a conformity assessment.

cases.text: An online clothing store adds a chatbot that answers questions about returns.
cases.explanation: Customers must be told they are interacting with an AI system.

cases.text: A grocery chain uses a model to forecast how many crates of apples each warehouse will need next week.
cases.explanation: Inventory forecasting carries no mandatory obligations beyond general law.

cases.text: A bank uses a model to decide whether to grant consumer loans.
cases.explanation: Creditworthiness evaluation and credit scoring are high risk.

cases.text: A brand publishes an AI-generated video of a spokesperson who does not exist.
cases.explanation: Synthetic media carries a disclosure obligation.

prompt: A Montréal resident is refused car insurance by a fully automated system. Identify which Law 25 right each step in the case relies on.

options.label: Right to human review and contestation

cases.text: The refusal email says, at the moment it is sent, that no person was involved in the decision.
cases.explanation: The individual must be informed of the automated decision no later than when it is communicated.

cases.text: The resident asks which factors weighed most and learns that the postal code and the number of past claims drove the result.
cases.explanation: On request, the enterprise must give the reasons and the principal factors and parameters.

cases.text: The resident finds that the insurer's file lists two past claims instead of one and asks for the record to be corrected.
cases.explanation: The same right covers the personal information used and its rectification.

cases.text: The resident sends a letter explaining the circumstances, and an underwriter reviews the file and reverses the refusal.
cases.explanation: The individual can submit observations to a staff member able to overturn the decision.

prompt: Each case describes a firm's conduct or an FTC response. Identify which part of Section 5 enforcement it shows.

options.label: Deceptive synthetic media and dark patterns

cases.text: A start-up advertises that its software spots lying job candidates from a ten-second video, with no independent study behind the claim.
cases.explanation: Marketing a predictive capability without rigorous, independent evidence.

cases.text: A kitchenware seller posts hundreds of AI-written five-star reviews under invented customer names.
cases.explanation: Undisclosed AI-generated customer reviews are deceptive.

cases.text: A tenant-screening model rejects applicants with housing vouchers at high rates, the applicants cannot avoid it, and no benefit to competition outweighs the harm.
cases.explanation: Substantial injury not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by benefits.

cases.text: After finding that a photo app trained its face model on images collected without consent, the FTC orders the app to destroy both the images and the model.
cases.explanation: The remedy reaches the trained model and weights, not only the raw data.

cases.text: A subscription service's chat agent introduces itself as 'Megan from billing' and never discloses that it is software.
cases.explanation: An anthropomorphic bot impersonating a human is a deceptive practice.

prompt: A pharmacy chain is rolling out an AI refill-reminder assistant. Identify the NIST AI RMF function each activity belongs to.

cases.text: The board names a vice-president accountable for all AI systems and sets the company's tolerance for patient-safety risk.
cases.explanation: Culture, risk tolerance and executive accountability across the lifecycle.

cases.text: Before launch, the team lists who the assistant will message, where its prescription data come from, and which harms are foreseeable.
cases.explanation: Establishing the deployment's context, stakeholders, provenance and risks.

cases.text: Analysts test whether reminder accuracy differs between patients who read English and patients who read French.
cases.explanation: Quantitative auditing of trustworthiness metrics such as fairness.

cases.text: When a reminder bug sends wrong dosages, the team follows its incident playbook and switches the assistant off.
cases.explanation: Responding to measured risks through incident playbooks and decommissioning.

cases.text: Every pharmacist who supervises the assistant must complete an AI oversight course each year.
cases.explanation: Workforce competencies are part of Govern.

prompt: A travel company is preparing an AI booking agent for customers in Canada, the United States and the European Union. Put its compliance work in the order of the six-step workflow.

steps.text: List every AI system the company runs and every country whose customers will use the booking agent.
steps.explanation: Inventory and jurisdictional mapping come first.

steps.text: Check the agent against prohibited-practice lists and decide whether it counts as high-risk or fully automated decision-making in each market.
steps.explanation: Risk-tier classification follows once the systems and markets are known.

steps.text: Confirm that every dataset used to fine-tune the agent has a valid legal basis and respects opt-outs.
Run fairness, sycophancy and evaluative-invariance tests on the agent's recommendations.
steps.explanation: The NIST Measure and behavioral audit suite.

steps.text: Add plain-language decision notices and a button that sends disputed bookings to a human agent.
Assemble the conformity dossier, get sign-off, and switch on post-market monitoring logs.
steps.explanation: The conformity dossier and continuous monitoring close the workflow.

prompt: Each case shows a shopping agent at work. Identify the regulatory gap it exposes.

cases.text: A marketplace labels a paid listing 'Sponsored' exactly as the law requires, yet the platform's own shopping agent still picks it far more often than an equal unpaid listing.
cases.explanation: A human-visible label does not remove sponsorship bias once an agent reads the page.

cases.text: A user is told 'You are chatting with an AI', but nothing reveals that the agent's instructions name the retailer, not the user, as the party it serves.
cases.explanation: Current rules do not require disclosing whom the system prompt names as principal.

cases.text: A grocery site prints the price per kilogram on product photos for shoppers but returns package weights to agents only through a slow, paid lookup.
cases.explanation: Unit-price rules cover shelf labels for human eyes, not machine-readable data.

cases.text: A hotel site places its best-value rooms in the middle of a 100-item list, where agents are least likely to choose them.
cases.explanation: Exploiting lost-in-the-middle rank positions falls under the ranking gap.
